public.goal: Learn how memory really works, and build a study system that fits two schools at once: recall instead of rereading, spacing instead of cramming, mixed practice, explaining, a weekly plan you keep, notes that test you, self-paced study at a distance, exam technique, and a pace you can sustain for four years.

project.title: Your own study system, used for two weeks

blocks.text: Build your own study system, and use it for two real weeks with your own courses. Then report what happened, with real numbers. Keep private details out: no names of other people, no passwords, and no copied course material.
Your report needs these five parts.

items: **Your plan.** Your weekly plan for both weeks: fixed commitments from official sources, about 80% of free time planned, spaced sessions, same-day recall after lectures, at least one mixed practice session a week, and sleep as a fixed commitment.
**Your methods in use.** For one topic at each school, show your recall attempts, with predictions and first scores kept honest, your review dates and how each review went.
**Your notes.** One page of notes in your own words with cue questions and a summary, and how many cues you answered from memory a few days later.
**Your weekly reviews.** Both reviews: what you planned against what you did, what slipped and why, and the one change you made for the next week.
**What you'll keep.** Which methods you'll keep using, which you'll change, and why, judged by your own results, not by how each method felt.

blocks.text: Write it in your own words. Your own record is the point, so don't have an AI write it. This project is self-checked, and the app will record it that way.

rubric: All five parts are present, with real numbers from two real weeks.
My recall scores and predictions are recorded honestly, with first scores kept separate from corrections.
I did both weekly reviews and changed one thing each week.
I judged methods by my results, not by how they felt.
It contains no private details or copied course material.

lessons.pack: How to Study · How memory works
lessons.title: Why rereading fails
lessons.source: Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke · Test-Enhanced Learning (2006)
lessons.courses: Supports study in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Distinguish familiarity from what you can explain without notes, then measure the gap on real course material and use it to decide what to study next.
lessons.why: Time spent reading can feel productive even when the ideas disappear as soon as you close the page. A small check early in a study session can tell you what to practise while there is still time to fix it. You can use the same method on a lecture, a course reading, or a lesson here.

sections.title: Two ways of knowing a page

blocks.text: Before reading on, think of the last page you studied. With the page closed, name its main idea and one reason or example that supports it. If you can remember the page's appearance or the location of a heading more easily than its argument, you have already seen the difference this lesson is about.

**Recognition** means you can identify something when it appears in front of you. **Recall** means you can bring it to mind when the source is out of sight. You may recognise an explanation immediately when you see it, yet be unable to give the explanation in your own words. A heading, a highlighted phrase, and the previous sentence all supply cues while you are reading. Close the page and those cues disappear.

**Familiarity** is the feeling that you have encountered something before. It is useful for finding where to look, but that feeling alone cannot tell you which parts you could explain without help. **Calibration** means comparing how well you expect to do with how well you actually do on a defined task. A useful prediction sounds like “I expect to recall three of these four ideas,” because you can check it against a result.

sections.title: What happened when students put the page away

blocks.text: Roediger and Karpicke studied students learning short prose passages. After the first reading, some students read the passages again. Others practised producing the contents from memory without seeing the answers. Different groups returned for a final recall test after five minutes, two days, or one week. The useful comparison is what the groups could remember at the same delay.

At five minutes, repeated study gave better recall. At the longer delays, the students who had practised recall remembered more. Repeated studying also increased students' confidence about remembering later. The same activity could therefore raise confidence today while doing less for the result the students cared about several days later. The outcome depended on when memory was checked.

The study used prose passages and a recall test. A programming task, a calculation, or a security investigation needs practice doing that kind of work too. For example, after learning how to read file permissions, explain the meaning of a rule from memory and then inspect a file you own. Each action answers a different question about what you can do.

sections.title: Make a prediction you can check

blocks.text: Set a small target before you close the source. Pick four specific points, such as a definition, a difference, a reason, and an example. A section heading is a useful prompt, provided you keep the actual answer covered. Write down how many points you expect to get, from zero to four. Then put the material away and write your answers without checking as you go.
Worked example: checking an explanation about computer files
Use these four targets for a short passage on backups: what a backup is, why it helps when the original is lost, why a shortcut is insufficient, and how to verify that a backup can be used.

items: Predict 4 out of 4 while the passage still feels fresh.
Close it. Write that a backup is a separate copy, that you can recover a lost original from it, and that a shortcut points to the original. Leave the fourth point blank if it does not come to mind.
Reopen the passage and check each point. If those first three explanations are accurate, the closed-book result is 3 out of 4. The gap between prediction and performance is one point.

Revisit the missing idea: verify that a copy can be opened or restored. Close the passage again and explain that action in your own words. The first score remains 3 out of 4. Record the correction separately.

blocks.text: A score based on meaning works better here than copying the original wording. Give a point only when the central idea is accurate. If an answer is partly right or vague, write what was missing. The purpose is to decide what needs practice, so count guesses, blanks and errors honestly.

sections.title: Decide what to do with the gap

blocks.text: A missing point tells you where to reopen the source. Read that small piece, fix your explanation, and try it again with the answer out of view. If you go completely blank, use a smaller passage or give yourself a short cue such as the heading. Record whether you needed that cue. When the task is manageable, try it again without the cue.

Rereading still has useful jobs. Use it to understand an idea for the first time, repair a specific mistake, or confirm a detail. After that, put the material away and see what remains. A strong score right after reading is good information about that moment. Schedule another short attempt tomorrow or later in the week if you want evidence that it lasted.
Looking at the answer and changing a blank into a correct mark because it now feels obvious. Keep the original result and write the correction next to it.
Choose one real page from a course reading, or use a completed 4YOS lesson you want to keep. Use a passage short enough to read in about four minutes.

items: Write four prompts tied to the passage. Pick one main idea, one difference or relation, one reason, and one concrete example. Keep the answers separate.
Predict how many of the four you will answer accurately. Put the source and answer cues out of sight, then write your answers. Spend up to four minutes.
Check against the source and record your original score. Write one correction for each point you missed. If you got all four, add a new example prompt and check it the same way.
Reattempt a missed point after closing the source. Set a date for a brief delayed attempt on the same four targets, with prompts but no answers in view.

blocks.text: Record the actual topic, prediction, original score, one correction or new example, and the delayed attempt date. Keep private course material and personal identifiers in your own notes.

rubric: I used real material and recorded a prediction before attempting four prompts with the source closed.
I kept the original score separate from any answers I corrected after looking.
I recorded a specific correction or new example and set a date to check my recall again.

exercises.question: You predict four correct points and produce two accurate points, one vague point, and one blank. What belongs in your first score and what do you do next?
exercises.answer: Score 2 out of 4. Mark what the vague response lacked and why the blank matters, then reread those two pieces and retry them with the source closed.

exercises.question: A friend can identify the right definition from a list but cannot explain it from a heading alone. What has the friend demonstrated?
exercises.answer: Recognition with the available choices. The next useful check is to produce the definition or an example with those choices hidden.

exercises.question: You answer everything right after reading a page. How could you find out whether the same knowledge is available on a later day?
exercises.answer: Put a fresh closed-source attempt on a later day. Compare the delayed result with the immediate result using the same scoring targets.

summary: Recognition happens with cues present. Recall means producing the idea yourself.
Compare a prediction with a closed-source score to calibrate your confidence.
Reread a specific gap, then test the corrected idea with the source out of view.
Check again after a delay if your goal is remembering beyond today's session.

lessons.pack: How to Study · How memory works
lessons.title: Recall before rereading
lessons.courses: Supports every course in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Turn any study session into recall practice: close the source, pull the ideas out of your own head, check, and correct. Write questions that make you explain and use an idea, and rate flashcards honestly.
lessons.why: The last lesson showed that rereading builds a feeling of knowing that doesn't last. This lesson gives you the replacement. Recalling an idea doesn't just measure what you know: the act of recalling makes the memory stronger and easier to find next time. It's the single most useful study habit in this course, and it's why every lesson in 4YOS ends with a check and why passed checks become flashcards.

blocks.text: **Retrieval practice** means bringing information back to mind with the source closed. It works as a way of learning, not only as a test. Each attempt follows the same cycle.

items: **Close** the book, the notes or the video.
**Recall**: write or say everything you can, or answer a question.
**Check** against the source.
**Correct**: write down only what you missed or got wrong, then try that part again with the source closed.

blocks.text: Do it soon. You don't need to feel ready, and waiting until you do turns the session back into rereading. Try a first recall straight after your first read of a section.

Getting things wrong during practice is useful, as long as you check afterwards. A wrong answer that you then correct tends to be remembered better than an answer you were simply shown. What matters is the check. Practice without checking can strengthen a mistake.
What counts as recall

head: Recall
Not recall
rows: Writing a definition from memory, then checking it
Explaining a method to an empty chair
Working a fresh problem with notes closed
A blank page: "everything I know about binary"

blocks.text: The question you ask yourself decides what you practise. A question that asks you to recognise a phrase trains recognition. A question that asks you to explain or use an idea trains the skill an exam and a job will ask for.

head: Weak question
Stronger question
rows: What happens to what's in RAM when the power goes, and why does that matter for unsaved work?
How many values can one byte hold, and why that many?
When would the mean mislead you about a set of incomes, and what would you use instead?

blocks.text: Good recall questions usually ask **why**, **how**, **what if** or **what's the difference**. Write them as you read: turn each heading into a question, and answer it once the page is closed.
The blank page

When a topic is large, start with a **brain dump**. Take a blank page, set three minutes, and write everything you can about the topic, in any order. Then open the source and mark three things: what you got right, what you missed, and what you got wrong. The missed and wrong parts are your study list for the next session.

Making beautiful notes and calling that recall. Copying and arranging ideas while looking at them feels like hard work, but you're not producing anything from memory. Make the notes, then close them and recall.
Flashcards are recall practice in small pieces, and 4YOS makes them for you from each passed check. They only work if you treat each card as a real attempt.

items: Read the front, and **say or write your answer before you turn it over**.
Turn it over and compare.
Rate what really happened.

blocks.text: The rating is what decides when the card comes back. 4YOS uses a scheduler called FSRS. It brings a card back sooner when you struggled and later when it was easy. If you rate a card "Good" because the answer looked familiar once you saw it, the scheduler treats it as known. An inflated rating can delay the next review beyond what suits your real recall.

head: What happened
Honest rating
rows: Got it, but slowly or with a struggle

blocks.text: Flipping the card before giving a real answer, then thinking "I knew that". If you didn't produce it, it's Again.
Recall needs a fixed place in your routine, or rereading quietly takes over again.

items: **After a lecture or reading:** spend 10 minutes that same day writing what you remember, then check.
**At the start of a session:** before new work, recall the last session's main points from memory.
**Before an exam:** spend most of your time on questions with notes closed, and the least on rereading.

blocks.text: Recall can feel harder than rereading. Some difficulty is normal, and researchers call helpful effort a **desirable difficulty**, but difficulty alone doesn't prove anything is sticking. Judge by results: can you recall it correctly on a later check? If you keep drawing a blank, use a cue or review the answer, then try again.

warmup.question: What's the difference between recognising an idea and recalling it?
warmup.answer: Recognising means you know it when you see it. Recalling means you can produce it with the source out of sight.

warmup.question: Why keep your first score, even after you've checked and corrected it?
warmup.answer: It's the honest record of what you produced from memory. A corrected score hides the gap.

blocks.text: Use one real topic you're studying now, or an earlier lesson here.

items: Read one short section once, then close it.
Do a three-minute brain dump, with no peeking.
Open the source and mark what was right, missed or wrong.
Write three recall questions about the section, each starting with why, how, what if, or what's the difference.
Answer them tomorrow with the source closed, then check.

blocks.text: Write down the topic, what you missed on the first attempt, your three questions, and how you did the next day.

rubric: I recalled from memory with the source closed before checking.
I wrote down what I missed or got wrong, not just what I got right.
My questions ask me to explain or use the idea, and I answered them again the next day.

exercises.question: Rewrite this weak question: "What does CPU stand for?"
exercises.answer: For example: "What does the processor do that RAM doesn't, and what happens to each when the power goes?" It asks you to explain and use the idea.

exercises.question: You answer a flashcard wrong, then see the answer and think it's obvious. How should you rate it?
exercises.answer: Again. You didn't produce it, and an honest rating brings it back soon enough to learn it.

exercises.question: You did a brain dump on a topic and got half of it. What do you do next?
exercises.answer: Check against the source, write down only what you missed or got wrong, and retry those parts with the source closed.

summary: Recall with the source closed, check, then correct: the four-step cycle.
Recalling strengthens memory. It's a way of learning, not just a test.
Ask why, how, what if and what's the difference, not "what does it stand for".
Answer a flashcard before you turn it, and rate what really happened.
Recall should feel hard. That effort is a sign it's working.

lessons.title: Spacing it out
lessons.courses: Supports every course in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Spread study across days instead of cramming, plan when to come back to a topic, and explain why a little forgetting between sessions helps.
lessons.why: With two degrees and limited hours, when you study matters as much as how. The same total time, split across several days, leads to much better memory a week or a month later than one long session. Your courses build on each other for four years, so learning that lasts saves you relearning later. It's also why 4YOS brings flashcards and week-later checks back on a schedule.

blocks.text: **Massed practice**, or cramming, means studying a topic in one long block. **Spaced practice** means dividing the same amount of study into shorter sessions on different days.

head: Plan
Total time
How it feels
A week later
rows: Harder, as you've forgotten some each time

blocks.text: Cramming can get you through tomorrow's test. Research on spacing, across hundreds of experiments with words, facts, maths and skills, has repeatedly found that spaced study wins on later tests. The gap gets bigger the longer you need to remember.
This sounds wrong at first. If you forget some of a topic between sessions, why is that better?

A gap means that when you come back, you find out what you can really recall after some time has passed, instead of repeating something that's still fresh in your mind. In a single long session, the second and third passes through a topic happen while it's still in your head. They feel easy, and they add little. After a gap, each return is real recall work.

This is the same **desirable difficulty** you met with recall practice: what feels harder often works better. Spacing and recall work best together. When you come back after a gap, try recalling first. If you can't, review the answer and try again. Spaced restudy helps too, but recalling first shows you what has really lasted.
The forgetting curve

Over a century ago, the psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus measured how quickly he forgot lists he'd learned. Memory falls quickly at first, then more slowly. Each time you successfully recall something, the fall afterwards is slower. That's the reason a review schedule spreads out: each successful review earns a longer gap before the next.

spec.alt: An illustration of forgetting. Memory falls quickly in the first days after learning, then levels off.
spec.note: Invented numbers to show the shape of the idea, not measured data.

blocks.text: The numbers on this chart are invented to show the shape. Real forgetting depends on the material and the person, and that's exactly why 4YOS adjusts each card's schedule to your own ratings.

You don't need to calculate anything precise. A simple pattern works: review a new topic after about **1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month**, using recall each time. If a review goes badly, shorten the next gap. If it's easy, lengthen it.

How far apart should the first sessions be? It depends on how long you need to remember. Studies that varied the gap found that longer gaps suit longer goals. To remember for a week, reviews a day or two apart work well. To remember for months, gaps of a week or more are better. For an exam in six weeks, spread your sessions over all six weeks rather than the last few days.
Let the app do the timing

When you pass a check in 4YOS, its main ideas become flashcards, and the FSRS scheduler sets each card's next review from your ratings. A card you find hard comes back sooner, and an easy one later. Your job is to show up for the review and rate honestly. The week-later check on each lesson is spacing too: it tests whether the lesson held after a gap.
Your timetable is fuller than most students'. Spacing makes it easier, not harder, because many short sessions fit in gaps that a long session can't.

head: Situation
Spaced plan
rows: 10 minutes of recall Monday evening, again Wednesday, and again at the weekend
Read one section a day, and start each day by recalling yesterday's
An assignment due in three weeks
Start now, and do a small piece on several days, not one late night
Cycle through every topic several times, with gaps, from now on

blocks.text: Planning to "revise everything" in the last week. Spread the revision so each topic comes back several times. One pass per topic at the end is cramming in disguise.

warmup.answer: Close the source, recall, check, then correct what you missed.

warmup.question: How should you rate a flashcard you didn't produce, even if the answer looked familiar?

blocks.text: Use one real topic you've just learned at either school.

items: Do a recall session on it today, with the source closed, then check.
Put four review dates in your calendar: tomorrow, in 3 days, in a week and in 2 weeks.
At each review, recall first, then check. Write your score each time, out of the same number of points.
After the last review, look at your four scores. Did the topic hold better as the gaps grew?

blocks.text: Write your topic, your four dates and your four scores.

rubric: I recalled the topic today and set real review dates in my calendar.
I recalled first at every review, and recorded each score honestly.
I compared my scores and wrote what they showed.

exercises.question: You have 4 hours to prepare for a test in eight days. How should you use them?
exercises.answer: Split them across several days, for example 1 hour on four different days, using recall rather than rereading.

exercises.question: A review was very hard, and you got most of it wrong. What should happen to the next gap?
exercises.answer: Shorten it. Come back sooner, then lengthen the gaps again as it improves.

exercises.question: Why does rereading a topic after a gap waste the gap?
exercises.answer: The gap makes recall effortful, and that effort is what strengthens memory. Rereading skips the effort.

summary: Spread study across days. The same time spaced out lasts far longer.
A little forgetting makes the next recall harder, and that effort strengthens memory.
Return after about 1 day, 3 days, a week, 2 weeks and a month, recalling each time.
Longer goals need longer gaps.
4YOS times your flashcards from your ratings. Show up and rate honestly.

lessons.title: Mixing topics
lessons.courses: Supports every course in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Mix related types of problem in a practice session, so that you practise choosing the method, and know when blocking one type at a time still makes sense.
lessons.why: In a textbook chapter, every exercise uses the method that chapter just taught, so you never have to decide which method to use. An exam mixes everything, and deciding is half the problem. Mixing your practice trains that decision. It feels slower and harder, which is why most people avoid it, and it's why the practice lessons in each 4YOS course mix topics on purpose.

blocks.text: **Blocked practice** means doing many problems of one type in a row: ten percentage questions, then ten ratio questions, then ten fraction questions. **Interleaved practice** means mixing the types in one session, so each problem could be any of them.

head: Blocked
Interleaved
rows: Score on a later mixed test

blocks.text: That last row is the important one. In Rohrer and Taylor's 2007 maths experiment, learners who practised blocked questions did better during practice, while learners who practised mixed questions did better on a test one week later. Practice scores can give a misleading impression of what will last.

When every problem in a row uses the same method, you only need to choose it once, then repeat it. You practise the steps, but not the decision. Interleaving forces you to look at each problem and ask: **what kind of problem is this, and which method fits?** That's the skill a real exam, or a real task at work, needs.

Mixing also makes you compare. Next to each other, a percentage question and a ratio question show their differences, and you start to notice the signals that tell them apart. Doing either kind on its own hides that difference.
It also brings in spacing. In a mixed set, the gap between two problems of the same type is longer, so each one is a small act of recall.
Judging a study method by how it feels during practice. Blocked practice feels better and scores higher in the moment. The test that counts is a later, mixed one.

sections.title: When to block, and when to mix

blocks.text: Mixing isn't always right. When a method is completely new to you, a short block helps you learn its steps first. Once you can do it with some help, start mixing.

head: Stage
What to do
rows: Meeting a method for the first time
A few problems of that type, in a block
Mix it with the types you already know
Fully mixed sets, like the exam itself

blocks.text: Mix things that could be confused, within one subject. Mixing statistics questions with each other helps, because you must decide between methods that look alike. Mixing one statistics question with one history question doesn't train any useful choice.
How to make a mixed set

items: Gather problems from three or more topics you've already learned.
Shuffle them, or take them from different chapters in turn.
Before solving each one, write in a few words what type it is and which method you'll use.
Solve, then check. If you chose the wrong method, note what should have told you.

blocks.text: Step 3 is the heart of it. Naming the type before solving is the decision you're training.

Keep two scores as you go: how many times you chose the right method, and how many answers were right. They tell you different things. If your method choices are poor, you need more mixed practice and more attention to the signals in each question. If your choices are right but answers are wrong, you need practice with the steps of that method.

head: Course situation
Mixed practice
rows: A statistics module with five methods
Each session, take a few questions from every method so far
Use the mixed practice lessons, then past papers, which are already mixed
Write small programs that each need a different idea: a loop, then a decision, then a list
Given a scenario, decide which threat and control fit before you look anything up

blocks.text: Past questions are naturally interleaved, because an exam paper mixes topics. That's one more reason they're the best revision material you have.

warmup.question: Why does a little forgetting between sessions help memory?
warmup.answer: Recalling a fading memory takes effort, and the effort strengthens it.

warmup.question: What should you do first when you return to a topic after a gap?
warmup.answer: Recall it with the source closed, then check.

blocks.text: Use a subject where you know at least three methods or topics.

items: Gather 12 problems, about four from each of three topics.
Shuffle them.
For each problem, write the type and the method in a few words before you solve it.
Solve and check. Count how many times you chose the right method, separately from how many answers were right.
For every wrong choice, write what in the question should have told you.

blocks.text: Write your three topics, your method-choice score, your answer score and one signal you'll watch for next time.

rubric: I mixed at least three related topics, shuffled.
I named the type and method before solving each problem.
I recorded how well I chose methods, and what signals I missed.

exercises.question: Rewrite this plan as interleaved practice: "20 percentage questions on Monday, 20 ratio questions on Tuesday".
exercises.answer: For example: 10 questions on each day, mixing percentage and ratio questions, naming the type before solving each one.

exercises.question: You've just met a completely new method. Should you start with mixed practice?
exercises.answer: Not yet. Do a few of that type first to learn the steps, then mix it with what you know.

exercises.question: Why does interleaved practice score lower during practice but better later?
exercises.answer: Each problem makes you choose the method, which is harder. That choice is the skill a later mixed test needs.

summary: Blocked practice repeats one method. Interleaved practice mixes types.
Mixing trains the decision: what kind of problem is this?
It feels worse during practice and works better on later tests.
Block briefly when a method is new, then mix.
Mix things that could be confused, within one subject.

lessons.title: Explaining it to yourself
lessons.courses: Supports every course in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Explain to yourself why each idea or step is true and how it links to what you already know, and use that explaining to find gaps before an exam finds them.
lessons.why: Knowing the steps of a method isn't the same as knowing why they work. Without the why, a small change in the question breaks you. Explaining connects a new idea to what you already know, which makes it easier to recall and easier to use in a new situation. It's also the skill a lecturer is testing when a question says "explain" or "justify".

blocks.text: **Elaboration** means adding meaning to a fact by asking how and why, and connecting it to things you already know. One form is **elaborative interrogation**: for each fact, ask "why would this be true?" and try to answer.

head: Fact
A why-question
An answer that connects
rows: RAM loses its contents without power
It holds bits as tiny electrical charges, which need power to stay
Recalling after some forgetting takes effort, and effort strengthens memory
It depends only on the middle value, so one extreme value can't drag it

blocks.text: Try to answer before you look it up. If you can't, that's useful: you've found what to study. Then check your answer against the source. A wrong explanation that you believe is worse than none, so the check matters here as much as in recall.

**Self-explanation** means saying, out loud or in writing, what each step of a worked example does and why it's there. Studies of students learning from worked examples found that those who explained the steps to themselves understood more and solved new problems better than those who just read the steps.
Worked example: self-explaining a solution
The textbook shows: $3x + 5 = 20$, so $3x = 15$, so $x = 5$.

head: Step
Self-explanation
rows: I subtracted 5 from both sides, to undo the $+5$ and keep the balance
I divided both sides by 3, to undo the multiplication by 3

blocks.text: Each line answers "what did I do, and why was that allowed?" If you can't say why a step was allowed, you've found exactly where your understanding has a hole.
Explain it to someone who doesn't know

A useful test is to explain the idea in simple words, as if to a friend who hasn't studied it, or to an empty chair. Where you reach for jargon, or say "it just does", you've found a gap. Go back to the source for that part, then explain again.
Explaining with the source open and reading it back. That's rereading in disguise. Close the source first, explain, then check.

Abstract ideas become easier to understand and remember when you tie them to **concrete examples**. For every idea, find or make an example, and then a second one that looks different, so you see what they share.

head: Idea
Example 1
Example 2
rows: A class of 50 grows to 60: up 20%
Your exam results seen by a stranger
A company's customer list leaked online
Debt that grows on its interest
A rumour where each person tells two more

blocks.text: Two different examples stop you tying the idea to one surface detail. If your only example of a percentage is about money, you may not recognise a percentage question about people.
Linking to what you know

Ask how a new idea relates to ideas you already have. Is it like something? Different from something? A special case of something? For example, ratio is like fractions, interest is percentages used repeatedly, and a byte is place value with only two digits. Each link gives the memory another path back.

In each lesson, try explaining a part yourself before asking Ayo. Ayo's explanation can help you check, or unstick you, but the learning happens in your own attempt to explain. Asking first skips the most useful step.
When Ayo or a book explains something, explain it back in your own words afterwards, with the page closed. If you can't, you followed the explanation without understanding it.

lessons.title: Planning a week around two schools
lessons.courses: Supports study in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Build a real weekly plan for two schools: start from what's fixed, fit spaced recall sessions into the gaps, keep space for the unexpected, and check the plan against what really happened.
lessons.why: Two degrees at once means two sets of lectures, readings, assignments and exams, with deadlines that don't know about each other. Without a plan, the loudest deadline wins every week, and spaced study never happens. A simple weekly plan turns the methods from the last lessons into actual hours. 4YOS's Today page does part of this for you, but the plan is still yours.

blocks.text: A weekly plan starts with things that can't move. These are **fixed commitments**, and you should record them from sources you can check, not memory.

head: Kind
Examples
Where to check
rows: Work, travel, family duties, worship, sleep

blocks.text: Put these in first. Then you can see the real free time, rather than the time you wish you had. Sleep is a fixed commitment too, as you'll see in the last lesson. A plan that only works if you sleep five hours isn't a plan.
Dates change. When a school changes a date, update the plan from the official notice, not from what someone said in a group chat. 4YOS's school calendar import keeps these in one place.

sections.title: Fit the study into the gaps

blocks.text: With the fixed items in place, decide how many hours of study you really have. Be honest: a free evening after a long day of lectures isn't three hours of good study.
Then give each course its share, using what you know works.

items: **Short and spaced beats long and rare.** Four 45-minute sessions beat one 3-hour session.
**Recall within a day of each lecture.** Book 10 to 20 minutes the same evening.
**Mix courses within a day.** Two different subjects in one evening is interleaving and keeps you fresher.
**Hard work in your best hours.** Put the most demanding work when you concentrate best, and easy tasks such as organising notes in tired hours.

blocks.text: Worked example: one weekday

head: Time
What
Why
rows: A self-study course: one unit section

blocks.text: That's under two hours of study, in four pieces, around fixed classes. A day like this, repeated, does more than one heroic Saturday.
Things go wrong. A lecture moves, power goes off, you get ill, a deadline appears. If every hour of your week is booked, one surprise knocks everything over, and you abandon the plan.

So leave part of your free time empty as a **buffer**. Planning about **80%** is a reasonable starting point, which you adjust after a week or two to suit how your weeks really go. When something goes wrong, the buffer absorbs it. When nothing does, use it to get ahead or rest.
Big tasks into small pieces

An assignment or a project due in three weeks isn't one task. Split it into pieces of under an hour, and spread them across the weeks: read the question and plan, find sources, write a first section, finish the draft, check and submit. Each piece is small enough to start on a tired evening, and starting is often the hardest part.
Writing "work on assignment" in the plan. It's too vague to start. Write the next concrete piece, such as "write the introduction, 300 words".
At the end of each week, take 15 minutes to compare the plan with what really happened. This is the weekly review, and 4YOS has a place for it in Goals.

head: Question
Why ask it
rows: The honest record, not the intended one
Too ambitious, wrong time of day, or a real emergency
Which deadlines are in the next two weeks?
So nothing arrives as a surprise
What one change will I make next week?
One change, not a whole new system

blocks.text: If you planned 10 hours and did 6, plan a little above what you managed, such as 7, rather than 10 again. A plan you keep beats a plan you admire. Over a few weeks, your plans will match your real capacity.
Two schools in one plan

When both schools need the same week, decide by what's due first and what counts most. If a topic appears in both, learn it once and practise each school's own questions. And protect the courses with no lectures to remind you, usually the self-study ones: without a fixed session in the plan, they're the first to slip.

warmup.question: Why spread three hours of study across several days instead of one evening?
warmup.answer: Spaced study lasts much longer, because each return after a gap is real recall work.

warmup.question: Why mix problem types in a practice session?
warmup.answer: To practise choosing the method, as an exam makes you do.

blocks.text: Plan your real coming week.

items: List every fixed commitment, from official timetables and course guides where you can.
Count your real free hours, and plan only part of them, about 80% to start, leaving a buffer.
Fit in spaced sessions for each course, with same-day recall after lectures and at least one mixed practice session.
Split any assignment due within three weeks into pieces of under an hour.
At the end of the week, do the four-question review, and write one change for next week.

blocks.text: Write your planned hours, your actual hours and your one change. Keep private details out.

rubric: My plan starts from real fixed commitments, checked against official sources.
I planned about 80% of my free time, with spaced and mixed sessions.
I reviewed the week honestly and chose one change.

exercises.question: You have 8 free hours this week. How many should you plan?
exercises.answer: About 6 or 7, leaving the rest as a buffer.

exercises.question: Rewrite "study for exams" as a plan item you could start on a tired evening.
exercises.answer: For example: "Do 5 past questions on percentages, notes closed, 30 minutes".

exercises.question: You planned 12 hours last week and managed 7. What should you do?
exercises.answer: Plan about 8 next week, and note why the rest was skipped.

summary: Put fixed commitments in first, from sources you can check.
Short, spaced sessions, with recall the same day as each lecture.
Plan about 80% of free time, and keep the rest as a buffer.
Split big tasks into concrete pieces of under an hour.
Review each week: what happened, what slipped, what's coming, one change.

lessons.title: Taking notes that work
lessons.courses: Supports study in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Take notes that make you think while you write them, and that turn into recall practice later: in your own words, with questions in the margin, and a short summary.
lessons.why: Notes can be a record you never look at, or a study tool you use for months. The difference is what you do while taking them and afterwards. Copying a slide word for word keeps your hand busy and your mind quiet. Notes in your own words, with questions to test yourself, make the lecture the first step of your recall practice instead of the last time you think about it.

blocks.text: There are two ways to take notes. **Transcribing** means writing down what's said or shown, as completely as possible. **Generative note-taking** means putting ideas into your own words: summarising, picking out what matters, linking ideas and noting questions.

head: Transcribing
Generative
rows: Copies the slide word for word
Writes the main point in your own words
Thinking about meaning during the lecture
Produces long notes you won't reread
Produces shorter notes you can use

blocks.text: Generative notes help because choosing and rewording forces you to understand. You can't put an idea in your own words without thinking about what it means.
Laptop or paper?

A widely reported 2014 study found that students who took notes on paper understood more than those using laptops, possibly because laptop users typed lectures word for word. Later, larger studies that tried to repeat it found the difference much smaller or unclear. A direct replication found no immediate learning advantage for handwriting. Both formats can record useful notes. So don't worry about the tool: summarise the main idea in your own words, then use a closed-note check to see what you can really explain. If a laptop tempts you to transcribe or to open other tabs, paper may suit you better. If not, type, but in your own words.

sections.title: A page that becomes a test

blocks.text: The **Cornell method** divides each page into three areas. It's useful because it builds recall practice into the notes themselves.

head: Area
Where
What goes there
When
rows: Main ideas in your own words
Two or three sentences on the whole page

blocks.text: The cue column turns the notes into a test. Later, cover the notes area, read each question on the left, and answer from memory. Then uncover and check. That's the recall cycle, built into the page.
Worked example: a statistics lecture

head: Cues
Notes
rows: Why does the median resist outliers?
Median = middle value when sorted. One huge value doesn't move it much, unlike the mean
Incomes in a street with one very rich person: the mean is high, but most earn far less
What do I report for skewed data?
Median, often with the range of the middle half

blocks.text: Summary: For data with extreme values, the median describes a typical value better than the mean, because the median doesn't depend on the extreme values themselves.
You don't have to draw lines exactly. What matters is having the notes, the questions and the summary, and using the questions later.
During a lecture

items: Write the **main ideas** and **examples**, not every word. If the slides will be shared, don't copy them, and note what the lecturer says that isn't on them.
Leave **space**, so you can add things later.
Mark what you don't understand with a **?** to sort out afterwards.
Write formulas and worked steps carefully, since those are hard to rebuild later.

blocks.text: After the lecture, within a day
This is where notes pay off, and most people skip it.

items: **Fill gaps** while you still remember: tidy unclear parts, resolve your ? marks, using the slides or a classmate.
**Write questions** in the cue column, using why, how and what if.
**Write the summary** at the bottom, with the notes covered if you can.
**Test yourself** once using the cues.

blocks.text: Then put the cue questions into your spaced review. They come back in a few days, then a week later, like flashcards.
Rewriting messy notes neatly as "revision". It feels productive and looks beautiful, but it's copying. Spend that time answering your cue questions instead.

For course materials and textbooks, the same ideas apply, with one change: read a section first, then close it and write notes from memory. This is recall while note-taking. Then reopen it, check, and add only what you missed.
Turning each heading into a question first gives you a reason to read and a cue for later. A heading such as "Types of malware" becomes "What types of malware are there, and how does each spread?".

warmup.question: What makes a good recall question?
warmup.answer: It asks why, how, what if or what's the difference, so you explain or use the idea.

warmup.question: In your own words, what does it mean to self-explain a worked example?
warmup.answer: Saying what each step does and why it's allowed.

blocks.text: Use your next real lecture or reading at either school.

items: Take notes in your own words, with a margin left for cues and space at the bottom for a summary.
Within a day, fill the gaps, write at least four cue questions, and write a two- or three-sentence summary.
Cover the notes, and answer each cue from memory. Then check.
Add the cue questions to your review dates for the next week.

blocks.text: Write your summary, your cue questions and how many you answered correctly from memory.

rubric: My notes are in my own words, not copied from the slides.
I added cue questions and a summary within a day.
I tested myself using the cues, and scheduled them for review.

exercises.question: Rewrite this transcribed note in your own words: "A variable is a named location in memory that stores a value which may change during program execution."
exercises.answer: For example: "A variable is a name for a value the program keeps, which can change while it runs."

exercises.question: Write two cue questions for a note about spacing.
exercises.answer: For example: "Why does spaced study beat cramming?" and "What should I do first when I come back to a topic?"

exercises.question: The slides will be shared after the lecture. What should your notes focus on?
exercises.answer: What the lecturer says that isn't on the slides, such as examples, explanations and warnings, in your own words.

summary: Copying word for word keeps your mind quiet. Your own words make you think.
The tool matters less than processing the ideas.
Cornell notes: notes, cue questions in the margin, and a summary.
Within a day: fill gaps, write cues, summarise, test yourself.
From readings: read, close, write from memory, then check.

lessons.title: Studying alone as a distance learner
lessons.courses: Supports any self-paced or distance course
lessons.goal: Run your own learning when there's no lecturer setting the pace: read the course guide, set your own deadlines, check your own progress, use other people, and ask for help early.
lessons.why: In a distance or self-paced course, much of the teaching is in the course materials, and there may be few required sessions. That freedom is useful for someone doing two degrees, and it's also the main reason distance learners fall behind: without a timetable, study slips quietly until a deadline arrives. The skills in this lesson are the ones a self-paced learner needs, and they're the same ones you'll need for self-study at work later.

blocks.text: In a face-to-face course, the lecturer decides what to cover each week, and the lectures remind you. In a distance course, the materials are the teacher and you're the timetable. The ability to plan, track and adjust your own learning is called **self-regulation**. It has three parts, and you've met pieces of each already.

head: Part
What it means
Tools from this course
rows: Set goals and when you'll work on them

blocks.text: The most common failure isn't lack of ability. It's that study without a fixed time gets pushed back, again and again, until it's too late to do well.

Start with the course guide or the official course page, if there is one. Check which sessions and deadlines are required. The guide is the closest thing you have to a lecturer explaining the course on the first day. Read it before anything else, and write down:

items: **What's assessed**, and how marks are split between assignments and the exam.
**Every deadline**, such as tutor-marked assignments, into your plan right away.
**The units**, and how many there are, so you can spread them out.
**How the exam works**, and what you're allowed to use.

blocks.text: Check these against the official portal and notices, since details can change between semesters. Don't rely on what you remember from another course.
Make your own deadlines

With the units counted and the exam date known, give each unit its own target date, working backwards from the exam. Leave the last two or three weeks for mixed revision and past questions. Then put the unit sessions in your weekly plan as fixed commitments, as if they were lectures.

head: Exam in 12 weeks, 18 units
Plan
rows: 2 units a week, with recall the next day
Mixed revision, past questions, weak topics

blocks.text: "I'll do the self-paced course when I have a free weekend." Free weekends rarely come, and one long weekend is cramming anyway. Give it fixed weekly sessions.
Studying alone doesn't have to mean studying lonely. Other people help you stay on pace and help you learn.

items: **A study partner or small group** can meet, in person or online, to explain topics to each other and test each other. Explaining to someone else is self-explanation with a listener. Agree on a fixed time, and set a topic for each meeting.
**Facilitators and study centres** exist to help. Find out what yours offers, and when.
**Course forums and class groups** are useful for news and questions, but check anything important against official sources.

blocks.text: A group works best when each person comes having already tried the material. A group that only shares answers to assignments doesn't help anyone learn, and it can break the school's rules on your own work. Assignments you submit must be your own.
Without a lecturer's questions in class, you need other ways to find out how you're doing.

items: Use the **self-assessment questions** at the end of each unit, with the material closed, and score yourself honestly.
Keep a short **progress log**: unit, date, recall score. A falling score tells you to slow down or revisit.
Do **past questions** from each school's authorised sources well before the exam.

blocks.text: When you're stuck, **ask early**. A question asked in week 3 is easy to answer. Ten unanswered questions in week 11 become a crisis. Write a clear question: what you're studying, what you've tried, and exactly where you're stuck. Then ask a facilitator, a study partner, or Ayo inside the lesson.
Ayo in 4YOS can explain and quiz you, but it doesn't know your school's rules or deadlines. Those always come from the school itself.

warmup.question: Which things belong in a weekly plan before any study sessions?
How do you take notes from a reading?
warmup.answer: Read a section, close it, write notes from memory, then check.

blocks.text: Use one real course where you study mostly alone.

items: Read its course guide, and write down what's assessed, every deadline and the number of units. Check them against the official portal.
Work backwards from the exam: give each unit a target week, and leave the last weeks for revision.
Put the unit sessions into your weekly plan as fixed commitments.
Start a progress log, and record your recall score after each unit.
Find one person or group to study with, or find out what your study centre offers.

blocks.text: Write your units, your target weeks and your first two log entries. Keep private details out.

rubric: I read the real course guide and checked the deadlines officially.
I set my own target dates for each unit, with revision time at the end.
I keep a progress log and have a plan for getting help.

exercises.question: A course has 15 units and the exam is in 10 weeks. Make a rough plan.
exercises.answer: For example: 2 units a week for weeks 1 to 8, leaving weeks 9 and 10 for mixed revision and past questions.

exercises.question: Your recall scores on a course have fallen for three units in a row. What should you do?
exercises.answer: Slow down, revisit the earlier units with recall, and ask about anything that's still unclear.

exercises.question: Write a clear question to a facilitator about something you're stuck on.
exercises.answer: For example: "In Unit 4, I don't follow why the median resists outliers. I tried it with my own numbers, but I'm unsure. Could you explain with an example?"

summary: In a distance course, the materials teach and you set the pace.
Self-regulation: plan, monitor and adjust.
Read the course guide first, and check details against official sources.
Set your own unit deadlines, working back from the exam.
Study with others, keep your submitted work your own, and ask for help early.

lessons.title: Exam technique and past questions
lessons.courses: Supports study in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Use a permitted past or specimen question to rehearse under relevant exam conditions, diagnose lost marks, and plan a targeted retry.
lessons.why: Recognising the topic in a past paper can make you feel ready. An exam also asks you to interpret instructions, use your time and show enough of the method to earn the available credit. A short rehearsal using your actual course can reveal which part you need to practise before the assessment.

sections.title: Find out what the current assessment expects

blocks.text: Recall the weekly planning rule from this course. Start with an obligation you can verify. For an exam, the authority is the latest instruction from the relevant school, course team or exam notice. Record which course it applies to and when you checked it. Write down the current duration, question choice, weighting, approved materials and answer format. An open-book assessment still has rules about resources and collaboration. If an exam format or allowed tool is uncertain, leave it as a question and check the official channel.

A past paper can show you how questions have been worded and how a previous paper was organised. A specimen paper can show an example structure. An older paper cannot establish that a current exam still has that structure or will ask the same topics. Use authorised releases, course-provided practice, or questions from your own course materials that you may use. Leave current restricted papers and files of uncertain origin alone. If no past paper is available, you can still practise with an authorised worksheet question and record what you cannot verify about the format.

sections.title: Read the task before choosing a method

blocks.text: Underline the action and the limits of the question. An instruction to state an answer may require only the requested value or fact. Explain usually asks you to give the reason or mechanism. Compare asks you to consider both items on a common basis. Interpret asks you to connect a result to what it means in context. Check your course's guidance for how those words are marked. If the question gives assumptions or a unit, carry them into your answer.

For a statistics prompt that asks you to calculate a proportion and interpret it, show which count is the numerator and which group is the denominator. Then say in words what the result is a proportion of. The number alone leaves the interpretation unfinished. In a computing or security prompt asking why a control is useful, first identify the specific problem the control addresses. Explain how it changes the situation and include any boundary named in the question. A list of definitions is only useful if it answers the task.

Set aside time to read the instructions, choose any optional questions and check your work. Divide the remaining writing time across the marks you are expected to attempt. If a paper allows 75 minutes, you reserve 5 to read and 10 to check, and the required answers total 60 marks, that leaves 60 minutes of writing. A 12-mark question starts with about 12 minutes and an 18-mark question with about 18. This is a guide. Adjust for sections that require setup, reading or calculations. Avoid allocating time to every question on the page when you are only required to answer some of them.

For practice, record a stop time and try a short set before attempting a whole paper. Match the resources and delivery format as far as you can verify. A timed calculation on paper and a typed response in a portal may call for different checks. When a question is taking too long, put down useful partial working where allowed, mark it for review, and move on. When you return, check unanswered items, units, question numbers and submission instructions before polishing the wording.

sections.title: Learn from the evidence you produced

blocks.text: Keep the answer exactly as it was at the stop time. Compare it with an official mark scheme or worked solution if one is available. Look for what actually earned credit, such as a method step, a supported conclusion or a correct interpretation. If you have only notes, record what you could verify and what is still uncertain. Do not assign yourself an official grade. Ask a course tutor about an ambiguous instruction or answer if you cannot resolve it.

Sort the missing parts into practical categories. A knowledge gap needs a brief review followed by a closed-source explanation. A misread task needs a new question with the same action word. A calculation error needs a clean run with the working visible. A timing problem needs a smaller timed set with a stopping rule. Preserve the original attempt, note the correction separately and choose a fresh question for a later retry. That second attempt gives you evidence that you can apply the correction beyond the question you already saw.
Reading the model answer first and then timing yourself on that same question as if it were new. Use that round to study the worked answer, then use a fresh question for your rehearsal.

warmup.question: What are the four steps of a recall attempt?
warmup.answer: Close the source, recall, check, then correct only what you missed or got wrong.

warmup.question: Why mix question types in a practice session?
warmup.answer: So that you practise choosing the method, as an exam makes you do.

blocks.text: Choose one real course you're taking. Use a question from its authorised practice materials and find the latest assessment instructions available to you.

items: Record the course, source and date checked. Note the current rules you can confirm and one point to verify if anything is unclear.
Select a small set from the authorised material. Write the action each prompt asks for and allocate reading, writing and checking time. Leave the answer key out of sight.
Run the rehearsal using the permitted resources. Stop at the planned time and preserve your original answer.
Review it with the published marking guide or source material. Label one issue by type and choose a fresh question to attempt later. If a score cannot be verified, record the issue without a score.

blocks.text: Save your practice record with the date, time budget, original outcome and retry plan. Do not copy restricted assessment content into 4YOS.

rubric: I used an authorised question and separated current rules from older paper instructions.
I used a time budget and preserved my first answer before checking.
I identified an issue from my own attempt and chose a fresh follow-up.

exercises.question: A paper gives 90 minutes, including 5 minutes to read and 10 minutes to check. The required answers total 50 marks. What starting time budget fits a 10-mark question?
exercises.answer: There are 75 minutes to write. Divide 75 by 50 to get 1.5 minutes per mark, then multiply by 10. Start with 15 minutes and adjust for the paper's sections.

exercises.question: You gave an accurate number, but the question also asked what it meant for the population named in the question. Which part needs work?
exercises.answer: Add the interpretation tied to that population. Keep the original answer as evidence that the calculation and the interpretation are separate skills.

exercises.question: An older paper asks for four answers, but the current verified instruction asks for three. Which rule belongs in your next mock?
exercises.answer: Use the current instruction. Practise relevant questions from the old paper within the current limits, or label the attempt as a different format.

summary: Verify current rules with the school before borrowing a format from a past paper.
Match the action in the question and show the reasoning it calls for.
Reserve time to read and check, then budget writing by required marks.
Keep the first attempt and use its specific gaps to plan a fresh retry.

lessons.title: Staying well while you study
lessons.courses: Supports study in any degree programme
lessons.goal: Protect the things your learning depends on: sleep, focus, breaks, movement and asking for help. Plan a pace you can keep for four years, not one you can keep for a week.
lessons.why: Two degrees is a long effort, and the biggest risk isn't one bad exam. It's running yourself down until you can't learn at all. Memory needs sleep. Focus needs breaks. Motivation needs rest and progress you can see. This lesson is about studying in a way your body and mind can keep up with, because how well you are affects how well you learn.

blocks.text: While you sleep, your brain processes and strengthens what you learned during the day. This is called **consolidation**. Research consistently finds that sleep after learning helps memory, and that missing sleep makes it harder both to learn new things and to concentrate.

That makes an all-night cram a poor trade. You gain a few hours of tired study and lose the sleep that would have helped keep what you studied. You also go into the exam with less ability to think clearly.

head: Choice the night before an exam
What happens
rows: A few extra hours at low quality, little consolidation, a slow mind in the exam
What you learned earlier is strengthened, and you think more clearly

blocks.text: Health guidance generally recommends that adults get at least seven hours of sleep a night. You may not manage that every night with two schools, but treat sleep as a fixed commitment in your weekly plan, not as the first thing you cut.
Attention fades during long sessions, and it's broken by interruptions. Every notification you check costs more than the moment it takes, because it takes time to get back into deep focus.

items: **Work in blocks** of about 25 to 50 minutes, then take a short break of 5 to 10 minutes. The exact length matters less than having a clear start and stop.
**Put your phone away**, in another room or face down and silent. Having it in reach pulls at your attention, even when you don't check it.
**Decide the task before you start**: "15 recall questions on Unit 3", not "study".
**Take real breaks**: stand up, move, drink water, look away from screens. Scrolling isn't a rest for your attention.

blocks.text: This fits what you know about spacing: several focused blocks spread across a day beat one long, distracted sitting.

Feeling tired and behind sometimes is normal. A pattern of feeling exhausted, unable to concentrate, and dreading study for weeks is a warning sign of **burnout**, and pushing harder usually makes it worse.
Things that help keep a sustainable pace:

items: **Rest on purpose.** Plan at least some time each week with no study at all. Rest is part of the plan, not a failure of it.
**Move your body.** Regular physical activity, even walking, is linked to better mood and better concentration.
**Eat and drink regularly.** Long study sessions without food or water make focus harder.
**Notice progress.** Your progress log and Library show what you've really done. On a hard week, look at how far you've come.
**Cut, don't crash.** When a week is too full, use the weekly review to drop or move things on purpose, before you run out.

blocks.text: 4YOS is built to support this. If you tell Ayo you're tired, Today becomes 15 minutes or rest, and nothing is lost: the plan moves.

Treating rest as wasted time and guilt as motivation. Guilt drains energy, and steady progress needs energy. After a rest, check whether you can focus and answer a few questions, and set the next block to what you can sustain.
Sometimes the problem isn't study technique. Money worries, family pressure, illness, or low mood can make study impossible, and those are reasons to get support, not reasons to blame yourself.

items: **Talk to someone you trust**: a friend, a family member, someone at your place of worship.
**Use your schools' support.** Universities have student affairs and counselling services. Find out what your school offers before you need it.
**Tell your school early** if illness or a crisis is affecting your studies. Many schools have procedures for this, but usually only if you speak up in time.
**See a health professional** for health concerns, including persistent low mood, poor sleep or anxiety.

blocks.text: If you ever feel unable to keep yourself safe, contact emergency services or go to the nearest hospital straight away, or reach someone near you who can help.

warmup.question: What is the buffer in a weekly plan for?
warmup.answer: So a surprise doesn't knock the whole plan over.

warmup.question: What are the three parts of self-regulation?
warmup.answer: Planning, monitoring and adjusting your own learning.

blocks.text: Look after the basics for one real week.

items: Put sleep into your weekly plan as a fixed commitment, and record how many hours you actually sleep each night.
Do every study session as focused blocks, with the phone out of reach, and note how many blocks you complete.
Plan at least one block of rest, with no study at all, and keep it.
Find out what student support services your school offers, and where they are, and write it down.

blocks.text: Write your average sleep, your number of focused blocks, and where your schools' support services are. Keep private details out.

exercises.question: It's the night before an exam, and you're tired. What's the better plan?
exercises.answer: Light recall on the main points, then a full night's sleep, rather than studying through the night.

exercises.question: Rewrite "study for 4 hours" as focused work.
exercises.answer: For example: four 45-minute blocks on specific tasks, with breaks between them and the phone in another room.

exercises.question: A friend has felt exhausted and unable to concentrate for a month, and keeps pushing harder. What would you suggest?
exercises.answer: Rest on purpose, cut the load using a weekly review, and talk to someone, such as the school's counselling service or a doctor.

summary: Sleep consolidates learning. An all-nighter trades memory for tired hours.
Study in focused blocks with real breaks, and keep your phone out of reach.
Plan rest on purpose, move, eat, and notice your progress.

Ask for help early, from people, your schools and health professionals.
